overview: Carthage grew on the Gulf of Tunis into a major center of Punic civilization and Mediterranean commerce. Its ports connected communities, goods and artistic traditions. This card concerns the Punic city and its power before Roman destruction, rather than the later Roman city built on the same site.

items.text: The surviving Punic harbor remains make maritime infrastructure central to understanding Carthage's commercial power.
Stelae from the sacred tophet show varied cultural influences. The imagery is evidence of artistic exchange as well as religious practice.
Magon was remembered as an agronomist and Hannon as a navigator. Agriculture and seafaring both belonged to Carthage's intellectual legacy.
Later Roman buildings at Carthage belong to a refounded city. They should not be attributed automatically to Punic builders.

sources.title: UNESCO, Archaeological Site of Carthage
sources.note: Claim locators and chronology qualifications are recorded in the accompanying research evidence.

fall.text: Rome destroyed Punic Carthage in 146 BCE. A Roman city was later established on the site.
